prompt:
You maintain a running summary of a long engineering document that is being read part by part, so that a later reader can model the system in SysML v2 without seeing the earlier parts.
Update the summary with the new part. Keep, as compactly as possible: the full names of system elements, actors and items; every alias or call sign with the full name it stands for; which element produces, sends or receives which item; modes and normative requirements. At most 300 words.

Current summary:
Context: FAA NextGen program aims to increase capacity/efficiency of the National Airspace System (NAS). En route operations are efficient in fair weather but suffer in adverse weather (convection, winds, turbulence, snow/ice, low visibility/ceilings; ~70% of US delays). A 2015 NASA stakeholder survey found weather-related delays the most costly en route problem. System of interest: NASA Airspace Technology Demonstrations 3 (ATD-3) project, a suite of integrated ground- and aircraft-based technologies and decision aids that continuously search for more efficient weather-avoidance routes and respond rapidly to weather changes and Traffic Management Initiatives (TMIs). It targets en route airspace and enables continued en route and arrival metering in weather. Subset: NASA Dynamic Weather Routes (DWR) concept, focused on the cruise phase. DWR uses existing air traffic weather, airspace and traffic data, improved navigation/surveillance/communication/digital network technologies, and existing ATM automation to offset shortcomings of strategic flow management and forecast uncertainty. Expected benefits: time, fuel and cost savings. Current system (shortfalls): TMIs ensure aircraft avoid adverse weather and meter traffic when demand exceeds air traffic control (ATC) separation capacity. Diversions and metering are overly conservative due to forecast uncertainty and capacity limits in sectors adjacent to weather. Actors: FAA traffic managers designate forecast convective areas as Flow Constrained Areas (FCA) and may implement Severe Weather Avoidance Plans (SWAP), also called Playbook routes, to divert traffic. Playbook routes are identified 2-8 hours before the predicted constraint so traffic managers and aircraft/flight operators can prepare resources. They are geographically and temporally conservative, give forecast weather a wide berth and minimize later changes, which are complex and slow once SWAP routes are in play. Gap: no automation notifies traffic managers when constraints change and avoidance routes are no longer needed, causing longer flights and higher time, fuel and costs. No modes or normative requirements stated yet.

New part:
U0025: Additionally, these large-scale rerouting actions also tend to use a static approach by finding the best compromise between weather avoidance, controller workload, and route efficiency...prioritized in that order.
U0026: Due to the difficulty in applying changes, aircraft often remain on conservative routes which are not required for weather avoidance.
U0027: Modifying those routes for aircraft already in flight requires a lot of coordination and can be time-consuming.
U0028: And there is no automation in the current system to help operators identify workable opportunities for time and fuel- saving corrections to weather avoidance routes that have become stale due to changing weather and forecast uncertainty.
U0029: Air traffic controllers, airline dispatchers and pilots can manually identify and request or amend these conservative routes as things progress to improve efficiency.
U0030: However, the associated workload to do so is very high at a time when controllers and dispatchers are very busy.
U0031: Consequently, aircraft often remain on circuitous routes long after the driving constraint is gone thereby incurring costly and unnecessary delays, and fuel consumption.
U0032: Airline flight dispatchers must file flight plans at least 45 min before push-back from the gate using their best available weather forecasts, but in practice flight plans are typically filed 1-2 hours before take-off.
U0033: When SWAP routes are in effect, dispatchers determine which SWAP routes are applicable to a flight’s planned route of flight and file a revised route accordingly.
U0034: Efforts have been made to apply more tactical operational tools to account for changes.
U0035: A good example is the Collaborative Trajectory Options Program (CTOP), which allows operators to file multiple routes on a single flight plan based on the amount of departure delay to which the flight is subjected and the operators associated preferences for that flight.
U0036: Although this provides a level of improvement over traditional single-route flight plans and rerouting procedures, it is still strategic in nature.
U0037: Therefore it provides no improvement in efficiency, flexibility and responsiveness to changes after departure.
U0038: Additionally, flight crews lack the tools to identify more efficient routes that will avoid congested airspace or conflicts with other aircraft.
U0039: And although they can identify more efficient trajectories using flight management systems and weather radar, they are unable to see convective weather anywhere beyond the limits of their on-board radar.

Return JSON {"summary": "..."}.
